title: Objects
summary: An object groups related information under named properties.

subtopics.title: Create an object
subtopics.explanation: Create an object with braces and pairs of property names and values, such as `{ name: "Mina", active: true }`. It is like filling a form with labeled answers. Use objects when several values describe one thing. Choose property names that make sense to someone reading the code later. For example, a profile object can group `name`, `email`, and `isActive` under one variable.

subtopics.title: Properties
subtopics.explanation: A property name identifies a value stored on an object. In `{ name: "Mina" }`, `name` is the property and `"Mina"` is its value. It is like a label attached to a field. Property names are usually strings, and they help code communicate what each value means. For example, use dot notation for `user.name`, but bracket notation when the key comes from a variable.

subtopics.title: Read a value
subtopics.explanation: Dot notation reads a property whose name is known in the code: `user.name`. It is like reading the field labeled “name” on a form. Use it for ordinary identifiers because it is compact and easy to scan. If the property is missing, JavaScript returns `undefined` rather than automatically raising an error. For example, check whether an optional property exists before formatting it.

subtopics.title: Choose a property
subtopics.explanation: Bracket notation reads a property using an expression, such as `user[key]`. It is useful when the property name comes from a variable or contains characters that dot notation cannot use. It is like looking up a form field using a label written on another card. Validate dynamic keys when they come from untrusted input. For example, a nested settings object is still shared when another variable references the same object.

subtopics.title: Nested details
subtopics.explanation: An object can contain arrays, functions, or other objects. These nested values help represent related information, such as a user with an address. It is like a folder holding smaller folders. Keep nesting understandable, and remember that assigning an object to another variable shares the same underlying object unless you copy it. For example, create a new object when updating shared state so other code can detect the change.

foundations.overview: An object groups related values under property names. A user object might hold a name, an email, and a setting. Think of it like a labeled form: each label points to one answer. Objects are common in JavaScript because names make data easier to interpret. Learn to create, read, and update properties, and remember that nested objects can be shared by reference.
foundations.whyItMatters: Objects group related information under meaningful labels. Understanding property access and shared references prevents accidental data changes and makes application state easier to reason about.
foundations.browserPerspective: Objects live on the heap, and variables hold a reference (a pointer) to them. The engine optimizes property access with hidden classes/shapes, so consistently structured objects read faster than ones whose shape changes constantly.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Configuration objects, API responses parsed from JSON, component props and state, options bags passed to functions, and lookup maps all use plain objects.
foundations.businessImpact: Clear object shapes make data flow predictable, reducing bugs in features that read or transform records — directly affecting product correctness.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Understanding properties, access patterns, and reference semantics prevents a large class of mutation bugs and makes data transformations (with keys/values/entries) straightforward.
foundations.performanceImpact: Objects are cheap, but keeping a consistent shape helps the engine optimize, and shallow vs deep copying choices affect both correctness and memory in data-heavy code.
commonUseCases: Modeling entities like users, products, and orders
Holding configuration and options passed to functions
Representing API responses parsed from JSON
Building lookup maps keyed by id for fast access

commonMisconceptions.myth: Copying an object variable copies the object.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It copies the reference — both variables point to the same object, so mutating one affects the other. Use spread or structuredClone for a real copy.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Object keys keep the order you insert them in for all key types.
commonMisconceptions.reality: String keys preserve insertion order, but integer-like keys are ordered numerically first — so don't rely on order for numeric keys.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Declaring a const object makes every property immutable.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Const protects the variable binding, but object properties can still be changed.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A missing property automatically has a null value.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Reading a property that is absent usually returns undefined; check the case your model permits.

visualExplorer.title: Building and reading an object
visualExplorer.caption: Step through creating an object literal, accessing properties, mutating it, and seeing reference semantics.

config.intro: Follow a `user` object from creation through access, mutation, and a reference gotcha.

steps.name: Create with a literal
steps.detail: const user = { name: 'Ada', age: 36 } makes an object with two properties stored on the heap.

steps.name: Read with dot access
steps.detail: user.name walks to the 'name' key and returns 'Ada'; unknown keys return undefined.

steps.name: Read with bracket access
steps.detail: const key = 'age'; user[key] looks up the key held in a variable and returns 36.

steps.name: Add a property
steps.detail: user.isAdmin = true assigns to a new key, creating the property on the fly.

steps.name: Iterate with entries
steps.detail: Object.entries(user) returns [key, value] pairs you can loop over to inspect everything.

steps.name: Share a reference
steps.detail: const copy = user copies the reference, not the object — copy.age = 40 also changes user.age.

codeLab.title: Count word frequencies
codeLab.instructions: Implement countWords(words) that takes an array of words and returns an object mapping each word to how many times it appears. Use an object as a tally and bracket access to update counts.
hints: Start with an empty object {} as your tally.
Use bracket access counts[word], defaulting to 0 with (counts[word] || 0) before adding 1.

keyTakeaways: Create an object with braces and pairs of property names and values, such as `{ name: "Mina", active: true }`.
A property name identifies a value stored on an object.
Dot notation reads a property whose name is known in the code: `user.
Bracket notation reads a property using an expression, such as `user[key]`.
An object can contain arrays, functions, or other objects.
